items.feedback: Correct. What makes it an agent is the structure: the model picks an action, the program runs it, and the result comes back, repeated until a stop. A longer prompt or a bigger model only changes what a single call can do.

Correct. The model only writes a request that names check_calendar and gives the arguments (laser cutter, tomorrow's date). The program around it runs the tool. Keep this split in mind when you write tool descriptions for your team.

You picked 'no change; it will eventually fix the bug'. That is tempting, but the agent is getting the same failing result 40 times in a row, so more steps add nothing new for it to learn from. A loop needs a stopping condition the program enforces, such as a step limit that stops and reports back to a person (option b). This also matters for your budget: every extra step is a paid model call.

Your 4 is right, and so is your count of the calls: three tool requests plus the final answer. But the reason says the model 'runs' the tools itself. It does not: each call, the model only writes a request for one tool, and the program runs it and sends the result back. The tool runs are not model calls. Rephrase it as 'the model asks for check_calendar, the program runs it', and your count still comes out at 4.

Correct. You gave both parts: the result goes back in as the model's next input, and the reason is that the model can use it to decide its next step. Your group-chat comparison works. The model only 'sees' a tool result once it is added to its input.

The name is part of it: the model does read the name check_calendar. But it relies on the whole tool description the program gives it: the name, what the tool does and the parameters it takes. A name alone can mislead (a tool called 'lookup' could mean anything). That is why writing a clear description for each of your tools is a core skill for the makerspace assistant.

summary: You have the loop down: q1, q2 and q5 are solid, and you explain the result-goes-back-in step well. Two things to fix. First, you believe the model runs the tools itself (q4's reasoning, M4): it only writes a request, and the program runs the tool. Second, you think a looping agent will fix itself with time (q3, M6), so it needs a program-enforced stop. Also, the model chooses tools from the full description, not just the name. Next step: trace the laser cutter request on paper again, labelling each step 'model writes' or 'program does', and add a step limit. Then try writing a full description for check_calendar.
